about: What this repo can distribute as a bank, and what it never distributes. This file is the source of truth, superseding the prose inventory in issue #219 — that one drifted from the repo and shipped wrong paths. It records the two things that cannot be derived. `bundles` are named groups of content that cannot be a package, because the tools that read it require it at a fixed repo-relative path. `exclude` records the paths deliberately left out and why. The bank's *package* set is not listed here: it is every workspace package the `pnpm-workspace.yaml` globs match, minus anything under `exclude`, so a package that is added, moved or renamed needs no edit (ADR 0039). A consumer's bank.manifest.json names packages and bundles; `bank:sync` resolves that selection to the transitive workspace closure of paths at the pinned ref, and reads nothing else. Paths here are prefixes — bank:sync has no per-path exclusion, so anything on `exclude` must be a path that no selectable prefix already covers. `tooling/bank/src/check-bank-paths.mjs` fails `pnpm lint` when a tracked root-level entry is in neither a bundle nor `exclude`. The first five bundles are flagged `alwaysIncluded` and together are one required set, split by subject: each carries a single argument for why its paths are required, and names the other groups its argument leans on. Nothing selects them and nothing can decline them, so the split changed what a reader can see and not what any manifest receives.

bundles.name: workspace
bundles.description: The workspace itself. These are the files pnpm, turbo and git read from a fixed repo-relative path, which is why none of them can be a package: without them there is no workspace for anything else to install into. `patches/` travels with `pnpm-workspace.yaml` because the workspace file carries a `patchedDependencies` entry pointing into it — sync one without the other and `pnpm install` fails outright. `.gitignore` is here on the same footing: `bank:sync` writes into a repo that has already built, so a consumer without it commits `node_modules/`, `dist/` and `.turbo/` on their first vendor commit. `.nvmrc` is the node version the whole workspace is built against, the fixed-path counterpart to `engines` in the root manifest — the optional `ci` bundle's setup action reads it as `node-version-file`, which resolves for a consumer only because this bundle is not the optional one. Depends on `commands` for the root `package.json`: pnpm treats a directory as a workspace root only when a manifest sits beside `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, and `turbo.json`'s tasks are the ones that manifest's entries drive.

bundles.name: commands
bundles.description: The root manifest and the script bodies its entries invoke. `scripts/` is one path rather than split per concern because the manifest's script entries are the only thing that invokes those files, and `package.json` travels with it for the same reason read the other way: the ten root devDependencies those scripts run on (turbo, prettier, lefthook, knip, syncpack, tsx, typescript, @turbo/gen, dotenv-cli, jsdom) are declared nowhere else. Deliver one without the other and half of it is inert. Only `name` in the manifest is consumer identity, and a field the bank never edits and the consumer sets once conflicts exactly never under three-way merge — the seed model `packages/platform/env` and tailwind's theme.css already use. A consumer that arrives with its own manifest omits it (docs/bank.md). `secrets.config.example.sh` rides here for the reason its readers do: `env:pull` and `env:push` are entries in this manifest, and the only useful thing they can say when the config is absent is which file to copy — a template a consumer never received is not an instruction. Its filled-in counterpart `secrets.config.sh` stays on `exclude`, because the mapping inside it is the consumer's own. Depends on `delegated-tooling`, which holds every package these entries and script bodies reach into, and on `workspace` for the `turbo.json` and `pnpm-workspace.yaml` they drive.

bundles.name: quality-config
bundles.description: The config the quality commands read from the repo root. Each is named by a tool that looks at one fixed path and nowhere else, which is why none of them can be a package: `lefthook.yml` is what `prepare` installs the hooks from, `knip.jsonc` what `deps:check` reads, `.syncpackrc.ts` what `deps:lint` and `deps:format` read, `.jscpd.json` what `dup` reads, and `.gitleaks.toml` is named outright by the `gitleaks` entry. `.prettierignore` is the one here reached from outside the root: every package's own `format` script names it as `../../.prettierignore`, so it is required by any selection with a package in it rather than only by the root's entries. Depends on `commands` for those entries — without the manifest these configure nothing, and without these the entries run each tool on its own defaults rather than the repo's.

bundles.name: delegated-tooling
bundles.description: The tooling packages always-included content delegates into. They are workspace packages, so the package derivation already offers them — but a selection could decline them, and the root `package.json` is always-included content, so anything it invokes has to arrive with it or a consumer's next sync leaves their scripts calling packages they never vendored. The bank is the sharpest case: the root delegates `bank:sync`, `bank:contribute`, `setup:wizard`, `check:bank-paths` and `check:bank-tokens` into `tooling/bank`, so a consumer that never named `@acme/bank` would lose the command that performs its next sync. `tooling/repo-checks` is the one a consumer feels soonest: the root delegates `check:exports`, `check:adrs`, `check:portable` and `test:policy` into it, and the first three run inside `pnpm lint` — so a selection without it fails the gate on the install that delivered it. `tooling/test-inventory` is the plain case, the root's `test:inventory` being nothing but a delegation into it. Two are delegated one step further out, through a script body rather than a manifest entry: `tooling/secrets-sync` is called by `scripts/env-pull.sh` and `scripts/env-push.sh`, and `tooling/workspace-graph` is imported by relative path from `scripts/resolve-infra.ts` and `scripts/resolve-compose-env.ts`. Those scripts arrive whether or not anyone asked for them, and anything an always-included script invokes is itself always included. Depends on `commands`, which holds the entries and the script bodies that name these packages, and on `config-closure`, which holds what their own manifests declare.

bundles.name: config-closure
bundles.description: The config packages the delivered manifests declare. Nothing always-included reaches into these: no root command delegates into them, and no always-included file imports them. They travel one level down, so that the manifests the other bundles deliver resolve — a bundle contributes paths and never walks dependency edges, so a package delivered that way arrives with a manifest whose `workspace:*` entries nothing else delivers, and `pnpm-workspace.yaml` is always-included, so the consumer's install resolves that manifest whether they selected the package or not. A bundles-only selection would fail `pnpm install` on an unresolvable dependency. `tooling/test-utils` is the clearest case of that argument and belongs to no other group: no always-included command or file reaches into it, but `@acme/secrets-sync` and `@acme/test-inventory` declare it, so the install that resolves one has to find the other. This bundle's content follows from `delegated-tooling`'s rather than from any argument of its own, and grows when that one does. Both directions are held by `tooling/bank/src/tests/backend/bootstrap.test.ts`.

bundles.name: scaffolding
bundles.description: The generator behind `turbo gen`, so a consumer can scaffold the packages it is creating with the same templates Trellis uses. It never touches packages taken from the bank — those arrive through bank:sync.

bundles.name: agents
bundles.description: Agent configuration, so a harness arrives already knowing the repo rather than being reconstructed. AGENTS.md is the one authored brief, with CLAUDE.md and .github/copilot-instructions.md as tracked symlinks onto it (scripts/link-agent-docs.sh recreates them on postinstall); `.agents/skills/` is the matching agent-agnostic skill source; skills-lock.json pins each skill to its upstream by content hash; .claudeignore is the committed source that scripts/sync-claudeignore.mjs compiles into deny rules, and .claude/settings.json is where those rules land alongside the authored permissions.allow, the disable* flags and the bootstrap hook — sync-claudeignore.mjs writes one of its keys, a human wrote the rest, and nothing else in this bundle carries them. scripts/register-skills.sh and scripts/link-agent-docs.sh are named explicitly even though the `commands` bundle's `scripts/` already covers them, so the bundle reads as self-sufficient.

bundles.name: ci
bundles.description: The workflows, the composite setup action every job calls, and the dependency-update configuration. These live under `.github/` rather than in a tooling package because GitHub only loads workflows from that fixed repo-relative path — the reason this is a bundle and not a package. `.github/actions/setup` is the one path-flexible piece (`uses:` takes any repo path) and is kept beside the workflows that are its only consumer. Named as three paths rather than `.github/` wholesale so the directory splits by concern: the only other thing in it is copilot-instructions.md, a per-harness entry point belonging to the `agents` bundle.

bundles.name: docs
bundles.description: The repo-wide ADRs, the agent protocol docs, the testing doctrine and the mounting recipes, which AGENTS.md links into by relative path — so taking the agents bundle without this one leaves those links dangling. Not the reasoning behind the packages: a package's own ADRs live in its `docs/adr/` and travel with the package, so a selection is self-contained without this bundle. Named as five paths rather than `docs/` wholesale because the directory divides by audience. These five state rules, which is what a consumer wants. The rest of `docs/` describes *this* repo to a reader — its doc index, its first-run walkthrough, its inventory of what Trellis ships, its task graphs — and is on `exclude` for the reason README.md is. `docs/bank.md` is the one file here that names Trellis deliberately: it is addressed to a consumer about consuming Trellis, so it is the how-to for the mechanism rather than a description of the repo. A doc added to `docs/` is undistributed until it is named here, which is the same trade the `ci` and `agents` bundles already make.

bundles.name: infra
bundles.description: The local dev stack: the compose file plus the assets it mounts. Selected automatically when any selected package declares `acme.infra` in its package.json — derived from the graph, never a hardcoded list (scripts/resolve-infra.ts is the same convention). The scripts that drive it (compose.sh, infra.sh, infra-up.sh, resolve-compose-env.ts, resolve-infra.ts) come from the always-included `commands` bundle, so `pnpm infra:up` always finds the compose file its `-f deploy/compose.yaml` names.

exclude.reason: Repository identity — a consumer's front page is never ours.
Repository identity — the consumer's licensing is its own decision.
An index of this repo's packages. A consumer takes a subset, so ours would be wrong on arrival; each package's own CONTEXT.md travels with it.

Repository identity, one level in — the front matter of *this* repo's docs. It indexes files a consumer's selection may not include and opens by linking the root README the bank already withholds. A consumer's docs index is its own.
A first run of this repo: its apps, its ports, its env files. A consumer's first run is docs/bank.md instead, and a walkthrough of someone else's project is wrong from step one.
The inventory of everything Trellis ships. A consumer takes a subset, so the page is wrong on arrival — the same reason CONTEXT-MAP.md is withheld.
A rendered graph of this repo's turbo tasks over this repo's packages. Derivable from any workspace, so a consumer's own is a `pnpm graph` away and ours is stale on arrival.
The same graph unpruned, stale for the same reason.

Its header says committed and non-secret, which is true and misleading: it maps secret names to each app's env file. A consumer rewrites the mapping wholesale while Trellis edits the same lines whenever it adds an app.

Consumer identity, on the reasoning that excludes `apps/`: the build context belongs to the app being imaged, and what to keep out of it follows from that app's Dockerfile — which the bank never distributes. Ours excludes `.env.local` and `.env.*.local` but not `.env`, so distributing it would put a consumer's `.env` back into their build context on whichever sync overwrote the line they added. A file the consumer must own is one the bank must not send.
Resolved from the consumer's own manifest set. Syncing ours would pin packages it does not have.

An app is the consumer's own. The bank distributes packages and configuration and never an app — `pnpm prune <app>` is the separate path for starting from a Trellis app, and #240 puts producing a runnable application out of scope.

Symlinks, generated by scripts/register-skills.sh on postinstall from .agents/skills/. Vendoring them ships links a consumer has to recreate anyway, and the run that recreates them is already in the `agents` bundle. Everything else under .claude is taken: settings.json is authored and rides in that bundle, and .claude/worktrees/ is gitignored local scratch that no sync ever sees.
Editor preferences — developer-local, and a consumer's team decides its own.

The bank's inventory of itself. bank:sync reads it out of the fetched bank tree at `ref`, never off the consumer's disk, so vendoring it would put a second, always-staler copy in a repo that already reads the authoritative one.
